definition: Neutralize means to cancel out the effect of something or make it harmless.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word neutralize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know neutralize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The negotiator neutralized the rival firm's biggest bargaining chip by publishing the disputed report herself.
Weakening a threat is milder than neutralizing it — the danger is smaller, but it can still bite.
Eliminating goes even further than neutralizing — a neutralized threat still exists, just harmless, while an eliminated one is gone entirely.

To defuse is to take the tension out of a situation before it blows up — the danger drained is emotional: tempers, panics, crises of nerve. Neutralize aims at capability rather than mood: a neutralized threat — a venom, a weapon, an argument — still exists but can no longer do anything. You defuse feelings; you neutralize threats.

To disarm is to take the weapons, or the hostility, away from someone who holds them; a guard disarms an intruder, a warm answer disarms a critic. Neutralize is broader: it leaves any threat harmless at its source, whether or not anything is taken away. You disarm a holder; you neutralize the threat itself.

Neutralize means to cancel out the effect of something or make it harmless.
The castle's designers neutralized the battering ram before one was ever built: the approach path turns twice, too tightly for any ram to swing.
Neutralize goes to the source: the threat itself is left harmless, unable to do what it was going to do.
That is what separates it from merely opposing something — a neutralized venom, alarm, or argument isn't fought; it's switched off.
Neutralize is the word for switching a threat off at the source — chemists neutralize acids, defenders neutralize an attack, diplomats neutralize a crisis.
Its unit-mate counteract fights an effect to a draw while the source keeps running; neutralize reaches the source and leaves it harmless.
Use 'defuse' when what's being drained is tension rather than capability.

The worm that crippled the county's library computers in March was never actually removed from most of them.
Instead, the volunteer security team found a cheaper path: a patch that would neutralize it where it sat.
The malicious code still shows up in every scan -- thousands of copies, intact, dormant on aging machines the county cannot afford to replace.
But the patch closed the one channel the worm used to act, so a program that once wiped whole catalogs overnight now cannot touch a single file.
Librarians call it the paradox of the fix: the threat is still there and always will be, and it no longer matters at all.
